body: A region is a geographical area containing at least one datacenter, usually several nearby ones networked with low latency. Most regions are paired with another region in the same geography, at least 300 miles away. If a region suffers a disaster, services can fail over to its pair, but not every service replicates data automatically. Planned updates roll out to pairs one region at a time. Sovereign regions are isolated instances of Azure for compliance or legal needs, such as US government regions and the China regions run with 21Vianet.
author: claude

body: Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within an Azure region, each with independent power, cooling and networking, connected by high-speed private fiber. Each zone is an isolation boundary, so if one goes down the others keep working. Regions that support zones have at least three. Not all regions support zones. Zonal services, like VMs, are pinned to a zone. Zone-redundant services, like zone-redundant storage, are replicated across zones automatically.
author: claude

body: Azure datacenters are facilities with servers in racks and dedicated power, cooling and networking. Customers do not work with individual datacenters directly. Datacenters are grouped into regions, and within regions into availability zones. A region contains at least one datacenter, and often several that are close together and joined by a low-latency network. Some services and VM features are only available in certain regions, while global services such as Microsoft Entra ID and Azure DNS do not need a region.
author: claude

body: A resource is the basic building block of Azure. Anything you create, provision or deploy is a resource. Every resource must belong to exactly one resource group, although some resources can be moved between groups. Resource groups cannot be nested and cannot be renamed after creation. Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it, and actions such as granting access apply to all the resources in the group, so groups work well for things that share a lifecycle.
author: claude

body: A subscription is a unit of management, billing and scale. It gives access to Azure products and services and is a billing unit: Azure produces separate billing reports and invoices for each subscription. A subscription links to an Azure account, an identity in Microsoft Entra ID or a directory it trusts. An account can have several subscriptions, but needs only one. Azure also applies access-management policies at the subscription level, so a subscription is an access boundary too.
author: claude

body: Management groups sit above subscriptions and help you manage access, policy and compliance across many subscriptions. All subscriptions in a management group automatically inherit its conditions. Every Microsoft Entra tenant has a single top-level Tenant Root Group. Management groups can be nested up to six levels deep, not counting the root or subscription level, and one directory supports up to 10,000 management groups. Each management group and subscription can have only one parent.
author: claude

body: The Azure management hierarchy runs from top to bottom: the Tenant Root Group, then management groups, then subscriptions, then resource groups, then resources. Policies and access granted at a higher level are inherited downward. A policy set on a management group applies to every subscription under it and cannot be overridden by the owner of a resource or subscription. A resource group holds resources, and a subscription holds resource groups.
author: claude
